title: gateway-collector-orchestration-strategy-tf-adapter
content:
Purpose:
This is a working proposal and runbook for orchestrating OpenTelemetry collectors behind the customer gateway in VPC/on-prem private deployments, with a Terraform adapter pattern to smooth upgrades. It focuses on coordinating metrics (Prometheus), dashboards (Grafana), traces and logs (OTEL/Fluent/rsyslog), and safe lifecycle migration for customers with strict network controls.

Context / problem statement:
- Private deployments are highly heterogeneous: customers run hardened gateways, restricted egress, and either an internal metrics scrape tower or push-based telemetry.
- Upgrading collector binaries or changing topology (sidecar -> central collector -> gateway-proxy) often requires network policy and firewall changes and has caused multi-hour incidents in the past.
- Terraform modules are currently per-customer forks or ad-hoc patches which make cross-customer upgrades risky. We need a migration path that lets us introduce a new collector orchestration model with minimal blast radius.

Goals (non-exhaustive):
- Provide a compatible orchestration strategy that supports both pull (Prometheus scrape) and push (OTLP/gRPC/HTTP) ingestion modes.
- Introduce a Terraform adapter shim so upgrades can be staged without rewriting customer configs.
- Define a clear canary and rollback plan with smoke tests and SLIs to detect regressions quickly.
- Document required network policy changes and provide templated firewall rules for common customer setups.

High-level architecture (proposed):
1) Existing: gateway -> customer network -> per-node sidecar collectors or direct exporter to vendor endpoints. Scrapes are either node-exporter + kube-state or remote scraping by an internal Prometheus tower.
2) Proposed: introduce a lightweight gateway-collector orchestrator that sits inside the VPC, exposed only to the gateway and the internal telemetry-only subnet: gateway -> gateway-collector (OTEL) -> local buffering layer (s3/kafka/queue optional) -> central scrapers/remote-write.
3) Compatibility layer: the orchestrator exposes both a Prometheus-compatible /metrics endpoint and OTLP/HTTP endpoints. For customers using scrape, we preserve scrape endpoints; for push customers we accept OTLP and translate to internal formats.

Compatibility matrix (short text form):
- Collector model: sidecar | gateway-collector | central-push
- Prometheus scrape: yes -> preserve; no -> use metrics-exporter in orchestrator
- OTLP protobuf v0.18 / v1.0: support both, with feature toggle in TF shim
- Kafka buffering present: orchestrator can forward to existing Kafka or fall back to local disk queue
- TLS / mTLS: orchestrator supports mTLS provisioning via customer KMS or mounted certs

Terraform adapter pattern (notes):
- Problem: customers have different module inputs and often pin module versions. Upgrading module logic to change resource shapes (e.g., replace aws_security_group rules) breaks state or requires manual state modifications.
- Adapter proposal: provide two layers: 1) stable public module with a fixed interface (module.redwood_obs) and 2) an internal implementation module that can be swapped using a thin shim resource set. The shim translates stable inputs into implementation-specific resources.
- Implementation notes:
  - module.redwood_obs (public): inputs = { mode, scrape_endpoints, otlp_endpoint, buffering, tls_mode, release_channel }
  - module.redwood_obs.impl_v1: current resources (sidecars, sg rules, scrape targets)
  - module.redwood_obs.impl_v2: new gateway-collector resources (lb, subnet placement, IAM roles, bootstrap config)
  - migration flow uses a staged tfplan that first creates new impl_v2 resources in parallel (coexistence) and then flips a traffic tag (DNS or internal routing) to prefer impl_v2. Only after a quiet period we destroy old impl_v1 resources.
- State considerations:
  - Keep resource names stable by using module-level resource aliases and lifecycle.ignore_changes for certain attributes during migration windows.
  - For security groups that must be updated, apply additive rules first and remove old ones only after validation.

Upgrade plan (phased):
Phase 0 - Prepare (2 weeks):
- Inventory existing ingress/egress rules, prom scrape topology, collector versions per-customer (automated scan script: infra/telemetry/inventory-runner).
- Create a per-customer migration branch with a copy of module.redwood_obs that sets release_channel = "canary".
- Share network change requests with customer security contacts.

Phase 1 - Deploy orchestrator in read-only mode (non-intrusive) (3 days per customer):
- Deploy gateway-collector in passive mode where it mirrors data but does not accept primary traffic. Use OTLP passthrough to avoid duplication risks.
- Verify metrics and traces appear in our staging Grafana dashboards.

Phase 2 - Canary flip (1 day):
- Redirect 3–5% of telemetry to orchestrator using traffic-tagging or DNS priority change. Observe for 6–12 hours.
- Run smoke tests (see below) and monitor token-level latency/ingest errors.

Phase 3 - Gradual roll (1–7 days):
- Gradually increase traffic to orchestrator in increments (10% increments, 12–24 hour windows). Run full regression suite daily.

Phase 4 - Cutover and cleanup (1–2 days):
- Flip full traffic when stable, then decommission old sidecars incrementally (drain + destroy).

Smoke tests and SLI checks (automated):
- Metric completeness: compare cardinality and scrape success rates (target: <1% drop vs baseline).
- Latency SLO for ingest: 95th percentile ingestion latency under 250ms for OTLP front-door in common cases.
- Error budgets: immediate roll back if error rate delta > 2% absolute or > 50% relative increase on trace/log errors.
- Grafana dashboard expectations: a test dashboard with synthetic metrics (heartbeat) deployed alongside to validate end-to-end flow.

Rollbacks and emergency procedure:
- If canary fails: revert traffic tag to previous flow (DNS or lb priority) and keep new resources in place for further debugging.
- If network rule change causes connectivity loss: pre-stage a temporary fallback rule (highly restricted) that can be applied via a single tf-apply (-var 'emergency=true').
- All rollbacks must be recorded in the customer migration ticket with timestamp, an owner, and the exact tf plan used.

Network and security checklist (template):
- Required ports opened (internal only): 4317 (OTLP/gRPC), 4318 (OTLP/HTTP), 9090 (prometheus exporter), 9200 (optional ES), ephemeral traffic to KMS endpoints if using external KMS.
- mTLS cert provisioning path: check if customer uses Vault/K8s-mounted certs or an external HSM. Document secret rotation window.
- Egress requirements: if orchestrator forwards to our central ingest, ensure customer whitelist includes our egress IPs or use VPC peering/private link.

Terraform snippets (illustrative, keep in repo as plaintext):
- Additive security group rule example: 
  resource "aws_security_group_rule" "allow_otlp_ingest" {
    type        = "ingress"
    from_port   = 4317
    to_port     = 4317
    protocol    = "tcp"
    cidr_blocks = var.observability_ingest_cidrs
    description = "Allow OTLP from gateway to orchestrator (additive)"
  }
- Lifecycle shim pattern: 
  module "redwood_obs" {
    source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//redwood_obs?ref=vstable"
    mode = var.mode
    scrape_endpoints = var.scrape_endpoints
    release_channel = var.release_channel
  }
  # impl modules are internal and may be switched by changing ref in CI-promoted tags

Operational runbooks (concise):
- Daily validation script: infra/telemetry/bin/check-migration-health runs prometheus queries and compares counts to baseline, posts an alert to #telemetry-migrations if anomalies.
- Post-upgrade audit: run terraform show and export state diff to audit bucket. Upload to customer migration ticket.

Open questions / risks:
- How to handle customers that enforce egress via a customer-managed proxy? Need proxy integration tests.
- Some older collectors do not support OTLP v1.0; we may need a translation shim which has CPU implications.
- Compliance for certain regulated customers forbids any buffering to external systems — we must support purely in-VPC retention and replay.

Action items / next steps:
- (Maya) build inventory runner and run across active private deployments by 2024-11-04.
- (Diego) prototype module.redwood_obs.impl_v2 and open PR by 2024-11-18.
- (Priya) draft customer communication template for security teams and circulate by 2024-11-08.
- Create a small pilot with one low-risk customer next quarter and schedule a dry-run upgrade in staging.

Appendix: quick checklist for on-call during upgrade window
- Pager triage owner: listed in ticket
- Quick revert command snippets: tf apply -var 'release_channel=stable' or restore DNS entry to previous record
- Logs to check: orchestrator stdout, OTEL collector metrics (/metrics), our ingest-bridge logs, customer's firewall logs

This doc is intentionally prescriptive but draft. Keep comments in-line and append findings from pilots below as we run experiments.
